questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Circle Given the Center and the Radius
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067768/assets/ae44c9f19c7afc26c399999105b7d17c6e2e6b3e020e7b419065a8514741dc9b.png)

 

Consider a circle with radius $3$ centered at the point $(3,0),$ shown above.

Current part:

Write the equation of this circle in the form $(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}={r}^{2}.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of a circle with radius $r$  centered at the point $(a,b)$ in rectangular coordinates in standard form is

$$
(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}={r}^{2}.
$$

In our case, the circle is centered at $(3,0)$ and the radius of the circle is $r=3$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2} & ={r}^{2} \\ (x-3)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={3}^{2} \\ (x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the equation of the circle in rectangular coordinates is 

$$
(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067768/assets/ae44c9f19c7afc26c399999105b7d17c6e2e6b3e020e7b419065a8514741dc9b.png)

 

Consider a circle with radius $3$ centered at the point $(3,0),$ shown above.

Earlier part 1:

Write the equation of this circle in the form $(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}={r}^{2}.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        $(x-3)^2+(y-0)^2=9$

Current part:

Write the equations of the upper and lower semicircles.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        Upper: $\,\,\,y=$

questions.worked_solution:
We make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9 \\ {y}^{2} & =9-(x-3)^{2} \\ \sqrt{{y}^{2}} & =\sqrt{9-(x-3)^{2}} \\ |y| & =\sqrt{9-({x}^{2}-6x+9)} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

* the equation with the positive square root, $y=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$, describes the upper semicircle, and 

* the equation with the negative square root, $y=-\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$, describes the lower semicircle.

Consider a circle with radius $3$ centered at the point $(3,0),$ shown above.

Earlier part 1:

Earlier part 2:

Write the equations of the upper and lower semicircles.

Current part:

Construct an integral that represents the area of this circle using rectangular coordinates.

questions.worked_solution:
Since  $y=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the upper semicircle  and  $y=-\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the lower semicircle, the area $A$ of the circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[(\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}})-(-\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}})]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}2\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider a circle with radius $3$ centered at the point $(3,0),$ shown above.

Earlier part 1:

Write the equation of this circle in the form $(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}={r}^{2}.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        $(x-3)^2+(y-0)^2=9$

Earlier part 2:

Write the equations of the upper and lower semicircles.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        Upper: $\,\,\,y=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        $\sqrt{9-(x-3)^2}$

                                        $-\sqrt{9-(x-3)^2}$

Earlier part 3:

Construct an integral that represents the area of this circle using rectangular coordinates.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${\int }_{0}^{6}$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        $2\sqrt{9-(x-3)^2}$                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                         $\,\,\text{d}x$

Current part:

Construct an integral that represents the arc length of this circle in rectangular coordinates.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${\int }_{0}^{6}$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                         $\,\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula 

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, ${f}_{1}(x)=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the upper semicircle and ${f}_{2}(x)=-\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the lower semicircle with $a=0$ and $b=6.$ 

First, we find the derivative of ${f}_{1}(x):$

$$
{f}_{1}^{′}(x)=\frac{3-x}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Substituting ${f}_{1}^{′}(x)$ into the arc length formula, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}_{1} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{1+[{f}_{1}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{1+\frac{(3-x)^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{\frac{6x-{x}^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}+\frac{9-6x+{x}^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In the same manner, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L={L}_{1}+{L}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{6}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Current part:

Given that the polar equation of the circle is $r=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta <\frac{\pi }{2},$ construct an integral that represents the area of this circle in polar coordinates.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                         $\,\,\text{d}\theta $
questions.worked_solution:
In general, the area of the region bounded by a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ and the rays $\theta ={\theta }_{1}$ and $\theta ={\theta }_{2}$ is given by the formula

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Therefore, the area of our circle is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}36{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}18{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}6\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
